We investigate the existence of normalized ground states for a biharmonic Choquard equation with exponential critical growth. By applying variational methods and a concentration-compactness principle tailored to the biharmonic case, we establish the existence of normalized ground states under specific conditions.

Historical documents are often damaged, making them difficult to read. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that combines image enhancement and text recognition. Our method utilizes a multi-task adversarial network to simultaneously improve the visual quality of degraded document images and enhance their text recognition accuracy. The network consists of an encoder-decoder structure that generates enhanced images, which are then evaluated by a discriminator. The discriminator's feedback is used to refine the encoder-decoder, ultimately leading to improved text recognition accuracy. Our approach is evaluated on the IAM and ICDAR2013 datasets, where it outperforms existing methods in terms of image quality and text recognition accuracy.

This research presents an automated system for extracting personal information from Indonesian identity cards using a combination of optical character recognition and natural language processing. The proposed method leverages the capabilities of Tesseract OCR to recognize text and employs a rule-based approach to refine the results. The system's effectiveness is evaluated through a dataset of 100 images, with an accuracy of 90% achieved.

This paper introduces a novel approach to channel estimation for IEEE 802.11p standard, leveraging the temporal averaging of received pilot symbols. The proposed method utilizes a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network to predict the channel impulse response, thereby reducing computational complexity and enhancing performance. The results demonstrate that the proposed scheme outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

Recent advancements in deep learning have led to the development of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), which have shown great potential in image processing tasks. This study explores the application of GANs in enhancing the resolution and colorization of astronomical images. By leveraging the capabilities of GANs, we aim to improve the visual quality and color accuracy of astronomical images, thereby facilitating more effective analysis and interpretation.

This paper presents a novel approach to training neural networks that bypasses the need for gradient-based optimization methods. By leveraging the universal approximation theorem, we demonstrate that a neural network can be trained without backpropagation or gradient descent. Our method involves a straightforward, iterative process that adjusts the network's parameters to minimize the error between predicted and actual outputs. We also provide a detailed analysis of the convergence properties of our algorithm and show that it can achieve the same level of accuracy as traditional gradient-based methods. Our approach has several advantages, including simplicity, robustness, and the ability to handle noisy data. We also discuss the potential applications of our method in various fields, including image recognition, natural language processing, and reinforcement learning.

The ECFA Early Career Researcher's Panel (ECRP) is a group of young scientists who serve as liaisons between the ECFA and the ECFA member institutions. The ECRP's primary goal is to foster collaboration and support among its members, who are responsible for organizing panel meetings, coordinating activities, and representing the ECFA at conferences. The ECRP's composition and structure have evolved over time, with the current panel consisting of 12 members from 10 different institutions. The ECRP's activities include organizing panel meetings, coordinating activities, and representing the ECFA at conferences. The ECRP's work has been instrumental in fostering collaboration and support among its members, who are responsible for organizing panel meetings, coordinating activities, and representing the ECFA at conferences.

A dual metasurface is designed to manipulate line waves in a specific way, enabling the creation of optical devices that can be used in various applications. The metasurface consists of two layers, each with a unique function, and is capable of transforming line waves into other types of waves, such as circular patterns or multiple beams. The design of the metasurface is based on a theoretical model that can be used to predict its behavior and optimize its performance. The results of the study show that the metasurface can be used to create a variety of optical devices, including a line wave splitter and a line wave multiplexer, and that its performance can be improved by adjusting its parameters.

This paper outlines a research initiative focused on developing a cognitive AI architecture that can be adapted to large-scale multi-agent collaborative learning tasks. The proposed architecture is designed to be open and expandable, allowing for the integration of new capabilities and knowledge. The research aims to address the limitations of current AI systems in handling complex, real-world tasks that require collaboration between humans and robots. The paper presents a detailed framework for the architecture, along with a discussion of the challenges and opportunities associated with its implementation. The research also highlights the potential applications of the architecture in various domains, including manufacturing, healthcare, and education.

A novel bias-corrected estimator for mean absolute deviation around the median is proposed, with its asymptotic properties rigorously demonstrated. The proposed estimator is then applied to assess the dispersion of COVID-19 mortality rates across European countries.

This study explores the potential of knowledge graph link prediction in enhancing relation extraction. We demonstrate that incorporating knowledge graph link prediction can significantly boost relation extraction performance, particularly when dealing with limited training data. Our findings reveal that knowledge graph link prediction can be effectively utilized to improve relation extraction outcomes.

The behavior of quarkonia in an anisotropic medium is investigated using a quasi-particle Debye mass model with finite baryonic chemical potential. The dissociation of quarkonia is analyzed in terms of the medium's anisotropy, spatial dimensions, and baryonic chemical potential. The results show that the dissociation of quarkonia is influenced by the medium's anisotropy, with the dissociation temperature increasing with anisotropy. The dissociation of quarkonia is also affected by the spatial dimensions and baryonic chemical potential, with the dissociation temperature decreasing with increasing spatial dimensions and increasing with increasing baryonic chemical potential. The findings are consistent with previous studies and provide new insights into the behavior of quarkonia in an anisotropic medium.

We investigated the magnetic properties of Tb3RuO7, a compound with a unique crystal structure, using neutron diffraction. Our findings revealed that Tb3RuO7 undergoes a series of magnetic phase transitions at 10.5 K, 7.5 K, and 4.5 K. The magnetic structure of Tb3RuO7 is characterized by the presence of alternating-bond spin-3/2 Ru chains, which are subjected to a non-uniform internal magnetic field. This results in the appearance of a partially disordered state in Tb3RuO7.

Deep learning models have achieved remarkable success in computer vision tasks, but their ability to generalize to new environments is limited. To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach that combines local feature extraction with a modulated periodic activation function. This method enables the creation of a versatile representation of local features that can be applied across various domains. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in multiple scenarios, including image classification, object detection, and cross-domain transfer learning.

We introduce a semi-generative model that combines cause and effect features with covariate-shift adaptation, allowing for the analysis of data influenced by both types of variables. This model is developed to address scenarios where some variables are subject to covariate shift and others are not. We derive a semi-generative error bound and propose a semi-generative empirical risk minimization method, which is shown to be consistent and convergent. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets.

Deep learning's success in solving complex problems is largely attributed to its ability to learn from vast amounts of data, but the underlying principles of its operation remain somewhat enigmatic. This paper aims to shed light on the geometric aspects of deep learning, focusing on the behavior of its key components, such as the loss landscape, the role of overparameterization, and the impact of optimization techniques. By examining these factors, we hope to provide a more comprehensive understanding of how deep learning works and why it is so effective.

We establish a connection between the principal factors of a lattice and its successive minima, and use this relationship to derive a lower bound for the principal factors in terms of the successive minima. This result is then applied to derive a lower bound for the principal factors of a lattice in terms of its determinant.

In the context of high-energy physics, the identification of jets is a crucial task.
To enhance the interpretability of machine learning models, we have developed a novel approach that combines expert knowledge with layerwise relevance propagation.
This method allows us to identify the most significant features within the jet images, which are then used to train a convolutional neural network.
By incorporating this expert knowledge, we have achieved a notable improvement in the explainability of the model, while maintaining its performance.
This paper introduces a novel family of Stirling numbers of the second kind, known as degenerate r-associated Stirling numbers, and derives their fundamental properties.

This study focuses on the irreducible and site symmetry induced representations of single and double layer groups, specifically ordinary and gray types. We have derived the irreducible representations for all 76 ordinary layer groups and 152 gray layer groups, along with their corresponding site symmetry induced representations.

We examine the conditions under which a momentum operator, defined by a Killing vector, is Hermitian with respect to the standard measure on a Riemannian manifold. It is demonstrated that this condition is met if and only if the divergence of the Killing vector is constant. Furthermore, it is shown that the self-adjointness of the momentum operator is equivalent to the Killing vector being a geodesic vector.

The Hubbard model, a widely used model in condensed matter physics, is known for its sign problem, which hinders the application of Monte Carlo simulations. To address this issue, we have developed a novel approach that utilizes a complex-valued neural network to mitigate the sign problem. By employing this method, we have successfully simulated the Hubbard model at low temperatures and achieved results that align with exact solutions.

We introduce a novel class of composite models that incorporate a composite flavon, which is responsible for generating the observed fermion mass hierarchy. In this framework, the flavon and the Higgs boson are treated as separate entities, with the flavon's role in fermion mass generation being distinct from the Higgs boson's role in electroweak symmetry breaking. The model's dynamics are governed by a specific potential, which is derived from the underlying composite theory. The model's predictions are consistent with current experimental data, and it offers a potential explanation for the observed fermion mass hierarchy.

Virtual reality technology has the potential to significantly impact human perception, but its use raises ethical concerns due to the possibility of manipulating users' senses. This paper explores the concept of perceptual manipulation in VR, examining its definition, underlying principles, and potential applications. We also discuss the implications of perceptual manipulation on user experience and the challenges associated with its implementation.

We've developed a method to adapt large-scale multilingual models to languages they've never encountered before. Our approach involves training a model on a substantial dataset of 100 languages, then fine-tuning it on a smaller set of 10 languages, and finally, testing its performance on 10 additional languages. Our results show that our method outperforms existing techniques, achieving a 10% improvement in accuracy for low-resource languages.

We've developed a 3D simulation of a rotating core that breaks apart into two parts, 
allowing us to study how the masses of the resulting binary systems are determined. 
Our results show that the masses of the binary components are influenced by the core's 
total mass and rotation speed, with faster rotation leading to more equal mass distributions. 
We've also found that the core's mass is not a reliable indicator of the binary system's 
mass, as the core's mass can be significantly higher than the combined mass of the binary components. 
Our findings suggest that the core's mass is not a reliable indicator of the binary system's 
mass, and that the core's mass can be significantly higher than the combined mass of the binary components.

This paper introduces a novel FastICA algorithm, M-ar-K-FastICA, which is specifically designed for non-Gaussian, non-symmetric, and kurtotic data. The proposed method is a modification of the FastICA algorithm, which incorporates the kurtosis of the data into the optimization process. The resulting algorithm is computationally efficient and can be used to analyze complex data sets. The paper also provides a detailed analysis of the algorithm's convergence properties and demonstrates its effectiveness through numerical experiments.

We investigate the relationship between finite model theory and propositional proof systems, specifically focusing on the Extended Polynomial Calculus. Our research demonstrates that the Extended Polynomial Calculus with polynomial-size proofs can differentiate between any pair of graphs that can be distinguished by a polynomial-time algorithm that does not rely on a specific ordering of elements. This finding is a refinement of an earlier result by Atserias and Dawar, which showed that the Polynomial Calculus with polynomial-size proofs can differentiate between any pair of graphs that can be distinguished by a polynomial-time algorithm that does not rely on a specific ordering of elements.
We introduce a novel infinite class of $\sigma$-elementary rings, where $\sigma$ is a countably infinite index set.

A key challenge in AI safety is to identify and address unfalsifiable claims, which are often made by AI researchers. These claims, such as the idea that AI will never be able to deceive humans, are difficult to disprove and can lead to complacency. To address this issue, we propose a method for analyzing unfalsifiable claims by breaking them down into their underlying assumptions. This approach allows us to identify the specific conditions under which a claim might be false, thereby making it easier to test and potentially falsify. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method by applying it to a range of unfalsifiable claims in AI safety, including the claim that AI will never be able to deceive humans.

This research focuses on developing a real-time system for identifying spatio-temporal events from geotagged social media posts. The proposed approach leverages a combination of techniques, including a novel method for extracting event-related information from text, a clustering algorithm for grouping similar events, and a classification model for distinguishing between different types of events. The system's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments on a real-world dataset, which show that it can accurately detect and categorize events in real-time.

The cross-correlation between the CMB and large-scale structure is a powerful tool for studying the early universe, but its potential is limited by the difficulty of analyzing the CMB's non-linear effects. We've developed a new method to efficiently calculate the CMB's impact on the bispectrum, allowing for a more accurate analysis of the CMB and large-scale structure relationship. Our method is based on a novel approach to modeling the CMB's non-linear effects, which we've found to be both accurate and computationally efficient. We've applied this method to analyze the CMB and large-scale structure relationship in the presence of various cosmological models, including those with non-standard inflationary scenarios. Our results show that our method can significantly improve the accuracy of the CMB and large-scale structure relationship analysis, and that it can be used to constrain a wide range of cosmological models.

We introduce a novel framework for Bayesian inference that guarantees robustness against adversarial attacks. This framework is based on a set of linear constraints that define a polytope, which is used to approximate the distribution of adversarial perturbations. By leveraging this approximation, we can efficiently compute the robust posterior distribution and make inferences that are both accurate and reliable. Our approach is demonstrated to be effective in practice, with experiments showing that it can achieve high levels of robustness while maintaining good predictive performance.

The COVID-19 pandemic has led to a surge in online rumors, which have caused significant harm to public health and social stability. To address this issue, we have developed a model to analyze the spread of rumors on social media platforms, specifically focusing on the characteristics of Chinese users. Our model incorporates the concept of "rumor types" and "rumor stages" to better understand the dynamics of rumor propagation. We have also proposed a new method for measuring the influence of individual users on the spread of rumors, which is based on the number of users they can reach. Our approach has been validated through experiments on real-world data, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness in identifying key users who play a significant role in the spread of rumors.

The effectiveness of spectral dimensionality reduction techniques in hyperspectral image classification is examined. A comparative analysis of various methods, including PCA, KPCA, LPP, and LPP-SDR, is conducted on the Indian Pines dataset. The results indicate that LPP-SDR outperforms other methods in terms of classification accuracy.

The growing size of language models has led to a pressing need for efficient compression techniques. This paper presents a comprehensive review of the latest advancements in compressing language models, covering both traditional and cutting-edge methods. We also provide a detailed analysis of the performance of these techniques and offer insights into their potential for future research.

We've developed a novel method to validate and refine protein structures by utilizing amide proton chemical shifts obtained from quantum mechanics calculations. This approach, called QCSCS, leverages the accuracy of QM calculations to assess the quality of protein structures. By comparing QCSCS values with experimental data, we can identify discrepancies and refine protein structures accordingly. Our results demonstrate that QCSCS values are highly sensitive to protein structure, making it a valuable tool for validating and refining protein structures. Furthermore, we've shown that QCSCS values can be used to identify and correct errors in protein structures, including those caused by incorrect side-chain conformations. Overall, our method provides a reliable and accurate means of validating and refining protein structures, which can be applied to a wide range of proteins and structures.

Deep learning models have achieved remarkable success in various fields, including image and speech recognition, as well as natural language processing. The performance of these models heavily relies on the choice of loss function, which is a critical component in the training process. This study investigates the impact of different loss functions on the performance of deep learning models, specifically focusing on classification tasks. We conducted experiments using multiple datasets and compared the performance of different loss functions, including cross-entropy, focal loss, and generalized cross-entropy. Our results show that the choice of loss function can significantly affect the performance of deep learning models, and that the optimal loss function depends on the specific dataset and task at hand.

We've developed a parquet theory framework that's based on the Hamiltonian formalism, which is applicable to a wide range of systems, including those with and without particle-hole symmetry. This approach is particularly useful for studying systems with strong interactions, where it can be used to analyze the behavior of fermions in various settings. By using a Hamiltonian formalism, we can derive a set of coupled equations that describe the behavior of these systems, which can be used to study the behavior of fermions in various settings. This approach is particularly useful for studying systems with strong interactions, where it can be used to analyze the behavior of fermions in various settings.

We have developed a first-principles approach to investigate the exciton condensation in materials, which is based on the self-consistent field theory of the one-particle density matrix. This method is applied to the study of the charge density wave transition in TiSe2, which is characterized by a significant energy gap in the one-particle spectrum. Our results show that the exciton condensation is the driving force behind this transition, which is further supported by the observation of a non-zero off-diagonal long-range order in the one-particle density matrix.

In recent years, text-based reporting systems have become a primary means for communities to report safety concerns. However, the underlying data from these systems remains largely unexplored. This research focuses on analyzing the interactions between users and dispatchers through these reporting systems, utilizing a dataset of 10,000 real-world calls for service. By examining the text-based exchanges, we uncover the hidden dynamics of these interactions, including the types of information users and dispatchers share, the factors influencing user reporting behavior, and the disparities in service provision across different communities. Our findings offer valuable insights into the complexities of these interactions and highlight the potential for leveraging this data to improve community safety and service delivery.

We investigate the magnetic properties of a superconductor with a specific symmetry, characterized by a unique order parameter, in the presence of a weak external magnetic field. Our analysis reveals that the magnetic susceptibility of this superconductor is influenced by the field's orientation, exhibiting a distinct anisotropy. Furthermore, we find that the magnetic susceptibility of a superconductor with this symmetry is significantly higher than that of a conventional superconductor with a specific isotropic symmetry.

We introduce Minimax Active Learning, a novel approach to active learning that minimizes the number of labeled examples needed to achieve a specific level of accuracy. Our method is based on a minimax framework, which we demonstrate is equivalent to a previously proposed active learning algorithm. We also show that our approach can be applied to a wide range of active learning algorithms, including those based on margin-based and confidence-based methods.

The evolution of Western music's complexity is examined through the lens of entropy and mutual information, with a focus on the compositional styles of Bach, Beethoven, and Messiaen. Our analysis reveals that the informational intricacy of Bach's music is comparable to that of Beethoven's, but significantly lower than that of Messiaen's. Furthermore, we observe that the informational complexity of Bach's music exhibits a consistent pattern across different time scales, whereas Beethoven's music displays a more nuanced structure, with varying levels of complexity at different time scales.

A reinforcement process is examined, where a process with multiple entry points is studied. The process involves selecting an entry point at random, then choosing a reinforcement point from a specified distribution. The process is repeated, and the asymptotic behavior of the process is analyzed. The analysis reveals that the process converges to a Poisson process, and the rate of convergence is determined. The results are applied to a specific case, where the process is used to model the growth of a network.

This paper explores the concept of harmony within the framework of computational ludics, a novel approach to understanding computation. We demonstrate that the fundamental principles of harmony in computational ludics can be derived from the more traditional notion of harmony in linear logic.

Reward learning is a crucial component of reinforcement learning, yet it poses significant challenges due to the difficulty of defining rewards. To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach that leverages visual feedback to facilitate reward learning. Our method, called Visually Assisted Cluster Ranking (VACR), utilizes a small set of human-provided clusterings to learn a reward function. By employing a time-efficient algorithm, VACR can learn a reward function that closely matches the human-defined clusterings, even when the number of required comparisons is significantly reduced. Our experiments demonstrate that VACR achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods while requiring fewer human comparisons.
We establish that a topological space's Smyth powerspace has a compact core-compact topology if and only if the original space has a compact core-compact topology.

We investigate the behavior of singular solutions in two-dimensional ideal fluids, specifically focusing on vortex loops with a pointed tip. Our analysis reveals that the velocity field near the tip exhibits a logarithmic singularity, which is consistent with the behavior of a two-dimensional vortex. Additionally, we establish the existence of a unique solution to the Euler equations for a vortex loop with a pointed tip, which is characterized by a specific asymptotic behavior at infinity. Our results also demonstrate that the vortex loop is stable under small perturbations, which is a significant finding in the study of singular solutions in ideal fluids.

We introduce a novel approach to estimate the average treatment effect, which combines augmented inverse probability weighting with neural network predictions. This method is designed to be robust against model misspecification and is demonstrated to be asymptotically normal. Furthermore, we develop a consistent estimator for the asymptotic variance and establish its validity through simulation studies.

The tau lepton's mass and short lifespan make it an ideal subject for investigating the Standard Model and potential new physics.  Recent advancements in tau lepton research have been made possible by the LHCb, Belle II, and NA62 experiments, which have significantly improved the precision of measurements.  This has led to a pressing need for theoretical predictions of comparable accuracy.  This article outlines the current theoretical challenges in tau lepton research, focusing on the impact of QCD and electroweak corrections, as well as the role of lattice QCD calculations.

A rotating annulus experiment is used to study the dynamics of baroclinic waves, and the results are compared to a numerical model. The experiment is designed to replicate the conditions of a rotating annulus, and the results are analyzed to understand the dynamics of baroclinic waves. The results are also compared to a numerical model to validate the experiment and provide a benchmark for future studies.

A novel reparameterisation of the Poisson process is introduced, enabling Bayesian inference for extreme value analysis. This reparameterisation facilitates the application of the standard Bayesian paradigm, allowing for the use of conventional priors and the incorporation of covariates. The approach is demonstrated through a case study involving the analysis of extreme rainfall data in the UK.

In offline reinforcement learning, researchers have developed various methods to address the issue of out-of-distribution data, but little attention has been paid to the impact of corrupted data. This paper introduces a new framework for handling corrupted data in offline reinforcement learning, which is based on a novel corruption model. The framework is proven to be robust against a wide range of corruption types and includes a practical algorithm that is demonstrated to be effective through experiments.
This research focuses on the one-dimensional heat equation with dynamic boundary conditions, specifically examining its logarithmic convexity and impulsive controllability.

This research paper explores the concept of out-of-distribution (OOD) text and its significance in natural language processing. We categorize OOD text into four distinct types and examine the challenges associated with each. Furthermore, we investigate the current methods for OOD detection and highlight the limitations of existing approaches.

We develop a theoretical model for Brownian molecular motors powered by inelastic electron tunneling, incorporating a Brownian particle's motion in a periodic potential and its interaction with a quantum system. This interaction is modeled as inelastic electron tunneling, where the particle's movement is influenced by the quantum system's energy levels. We derive a master equation for the reduced density matrix of the quantum system, which is then used to calculate the particle's average velocity and current. Our model is applied to a specific example, where we calculate the particle's average velocity and current as a function of various parameters, including the bias voltage and the coupling strength between the particle and the quantum system. Our results show that the particle's average velocity and current exhibit non-monotonic behavior, which is consistent with experimental observations. Our model provides a theoretical framework for understanding the dynamics of Brownian molecular motors powered by inelastic electron tunneling, and can be used to predict the behavior of such motors under various conditions.

We investigate the properties of one-way transducers that process words, specifically focusing on their ability to synchronize outputs. Our research reveals that a transducer can be modified to have a synchronized output if and only if it can be simplified to have a limited number of states without losing its functionality. Furthermore, we provide an algorithm that can determine whether a transducer can be modified to have a synchronized output and, if so, produce a simplified version of it.

We introduce a novel algorithm for efficiently calculating the generalized convolution of two vectors, $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$, with lengths $n$ and $m$ respectively. The algorithm's time complexity is $O(nm\log n)$, which is a significant improvement over the standard $O(nm)$ approach. This advancement is particularly beneficial for applications such as polynomial multiplication and string matching, where the generalized convolution is frequently employed.

The discovery of the first known T-dwarf, GJ 229B, in 1995, marked a significant milestone in the study of brown dwarfs. Despite extensive research, the atmospheric composition of GJ 229B remains a subject of debate. To resolve this uncertainty, we conducted a comprehensive analysis using the APOLLO retrieval code, which allowed us to determine the atmospheric properties of GJ 229B with high precision. Our results indicate that the atmosphere of GJ 229B is characterized by a temperature of 800 K, a surface gravity of 5.0 dex, and a metallicity of 0.0 dex. Furthermore, we found that the atmosphere of GJ 229B is dominated by molecular species such as H2O, CH4, and CO, which are consistent with the predictions of chemical equilibrium models. Our study provides a solid foundation for future research on the atmospheric composition of brown dwarfs and exoplanets.

The well-mixed model is found to be a useful approximation for predicting disease transmission in a city bus, particularly when the number of infected individuals is small.

Double-sided auctions are a widely used method for matching buyers and sellers in financial markets.  However, the complexity of these auctions makes them susceptible to errors, which can lead to significant financial losses.  To address this issue, we have developed a formal framework for verifying double-sided auctions, which enables the detection of bugs in auction implementations.  Our framework is based on a general model of double-sided auctions, which we have applied to verify the correctness of two prominent auction implementations: the one used by the New York Stock Exchange and the one used by the London Stock Exchange.

Using heavy quark effective theory, we analyze the properties of bottom mesons with $F$-wave characteristics. We calculate the masses of these mesons and their radial excitations, as well as their decay constants, and compare our results with existing data from lattice QCD and experimental studies.

We investigate periodic decompositions of the plane, which are collections of closed sets that partition the plane into periodic patterns. Our research focuses on decompositions with nonexpansive lines, which are lines that do not expand distances between points. We establish that such decompositions are equivalent to those with nonexpansive lines, which are characterized by having a finite number of lines that do not expand distances between points.

A novel approach to kernel-based learning for robust dynamic mode decomposition is presented, which can be applied to both linear and nonlinear systems. This method, called Linear and Nonlinear Disambiguation Optimization (LANDO), is a kernel-based learning technique that can be used to identify the optimal kernel for dynamic mode decomposition. LANDO is a flexible method that can be used to identify the optimal kernel for a given system, and it is shown to be effective in a variety of applications.

The chess community's collective knowledge is a vast and intricate resource, 
which we aim to analyze and quantify. By leveraging data from the Lichess.org 
platform, we develop a method to measure the intricacy of chess openings and 
determine their similarities. Our approach involves creating a graph that 
represents the relationships between chess openings, which we then analyze using 
various metrics. We also introduce a new method for comparing chess openings, 
which we demonstrate through a case study on the Queen's Gambit.

The discovery of millisecond pulsars in binary systems with white dwarfs has led to a growing interest in understanding their properties. By analyzing the timing of these systems, researchers can derive key parameters such as the mass of the white dwarf and the orbital period. A novel approach using the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) is presented to determine the most likely values for these parameters. This method is applied to a sample of 11 millisecond pulsars in binary systems with white dwarfs, and the results are compared to existing measurements. The analysis reveals that the AIC method can accurately predict the mass of the white dwarf and the orbital period, and that the derived values are consistent with existing measurements. The study also highlights the potential for using the AIC method to derive the masses of white dwarfs in other binary systems, and that the method can be used to test theories of stellar evolution.
We examine the characteristics of nonlocal constants of motion in Lagrangian dynamics of any order, specifically focusing on their relationship to Noether symmetries and the Euler-Lagrange equations.

This paper introduces a novel approach to 3D shape retrieval that leverages 3D sketches created in a virtual reality environment. The proposed method involves a two-stage process: first, a 3D sketch is converted into a mesh using a neural network, and then the mesh is used to retrieve similar shapes from a database. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through experiments on the ShapeNet dataset, which show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance.

HD 80606 b, a planet with a highly elliptical orbit, experiences significant variations in its star's brightness due to its proximity to its star. This unique behavior makes it an ideal candidate for studying the planet's atmosphere using the James Webb Space Telescope. To optimize the use of JWST's limited time, we need to accurately predict the planet's position in its orbit. We have developed a new method to refine the planet's orbital predictions by analyzing the timing of its star's brightness changes. By combining data from multiple observatories, we have been able to improve the accuracy of our predictions. Our results show that the planet's orbital period is 159.114 days, and its closest approach to its star occurs 1.000 days after periastron. We have also found that the planet's orbital eccentricity is 0.933. These refined predictions will enable us to schedule JWST observations more efficiently.

We investigate the possibility of isentropic perfect fluid collapse with a linear equation of state, focusing on the behavior of the collapse as it approaches the singularity. Our analysis reveals that the collapse is not viable for all values of the adiabatic index, but rather only for a specific range of values, which we identify as $\gamma \in (1, 2)$.

We apply the Iyer-Wald formalism to derive a general formula for the mass of an extremal black hole, which is then used to verify the mass correction formula for specific black hole types, including Kerr-Newman and Reissner-Nordstrom black holes.

In the context of motor learning, the End-Effect Exploration Drive (EED) is a novel approach that utilizes a dual-loop control system to facilitate the discovery of new movement patterns. The outer loop of this system employs a reinforcement learning algorithm to determine the optimal action, while the inner loop utilizes a model predictive control algorithm to execute the action. The EED approach is demonstrated to be effective in a simulated task involving a robotic arm, where it successfully enables the robot to learn a new movement pattern.

We introduce a novel extension of the Poincaré group, the colour Poincaré group, which incorporates a colour symmetry. This group is characterised by a colour Poincaré algebra, which we derive and use to construct a colour Poincaré symmetry for matter and gravity actions. We demonstrate that the matter action can be formulated in a gauge-invariant manner, and that the gravity action can be expressed in a gauge-invariant manner, thereby enabling the development of a colour Poincaré gravity theory.

We investigate the parameterized complexity of the upward planarity testing problem for directed graphs. Our research reveals that upward planarity can be effectively addressed in time proportional to $f(k)\cdot n^{O(1)}$, where $k$ represents the number of non-planar edge pairs and $n$ denotes the total number of edges in the graph.

In the field of visual navigation, a robot's ability to recall past experiences is crucial. However, the sheer volume of data it can remember poses a significant challenge. To address this, we've developed a novel memory selection method called MemoNav, which enables a robot to choose the most valuable experiences to recall. MemoNav operates by identifying the most informative memories based on the robot's current location and its intended destination. Our approach is grounded in a theoretical framework that demonstrates its effectiveness in reducing the amount of data needed for optimal performance. We've also conducted experiments using both simulated and real-world environments, which show that MemoNav outperforms existing methods in terms of data efficiency and navigation accuracy.

The advent of 4G technology has led to a surge in mobile data usage, necessitating the deployment of small cells to alleviate network congestion. This paper delves into the evolution of small cells from 4G to 6G, examining their historical context, current state, and potential future developments. It explores the challenges and opportunities associated with small cell evolution, including the integration of AI and machine learning, and the potential for 6G to revolutionize the concept of small cells.

We introduce a novel framework for studying complex systems, extending the concept of dynamical systems to hypergraphs. This approach enables the analysis of systems with intricate interactions, such as those found in social networks and biological systems. We develop a mathematical model for hypergraph dynamical systems, including a set of equations that describe the evolution of the system over time. We also explore the properties of these systems, including stability and bifurcation, and provide examples of their application to real-world problems.

We investigate the entanglement properties of local operators in chaotic systems, 
focusing on their operator length and entanglement entropy growth. 
Our analysis reveals that the entanglement entropy growth rate is directly 
proportional to the operator length growth rate, 
indicating a linear relationship between the two. 
This relationship is further supported by the observation that the entanglement 
entropy growth rate is independent of the initial operator's support size. 
Our findings are consistent with the concept of operator growth in chaotic systems, 
where local operators spread out over the Hilbert space, 
forming a complex entangled state. 
Our results provide a new perspective on the entanglement properties of chaotic systems, 
and may have implications for understanding the dynamics of quantum information.

The direct-decay component of the Hoyle state is measured using a Time Projection Chamber, which allows for a precise determination of the component's magnitude. The measurement is based on the analysis of a large dataset of alpha-alpha scattering events, which are used to calculate the direct-decay component's magnitude. The measurement is found to be in agreement with previous studies, which have shown that the direct-decay component is responsible for the majority of the Hoyle state's decay.

We investigate the dynamic fracture of brittle materials in two dimensions, focusing on the influence of intrinsic material length and time scales. Our analysis reveals that the oscillatory instability is primarily driven by the material's intrinsic time scale, whereas the tip-splitting instability is governed by the material's intrinsic length scale. Our findings are supported by a combination of phase-field modeling and numerical simulations.

This research focuses on finite-state channels with feedback and state information at the encoder, deriving an achievable rate expression for this scenario. The study also examines specific channel models, including the Gilbert-Elliot channel and a binary channel with state-dependent transition probabilities, to provide insights into the capacity of these systems.

We investigate the Rashba Hubbard model with attractive interactions, focusing on the Rashba coupling strength's impact on topological superconductivity. Our analysis reveals that spin-singlet topological superconductivity emerges at intermediate coupling strengths, whereas strong coupling leads to spin-triplet topological superconductivity. Our findings are substantiated by mean-field theory and quantum Monte Carlo simulations.

This paper outlines the details of the SEM-TAB-FACTS task, which is part of the SemEval-2021 competition. The task involves verifying facts within scientific documents that contain tables, as well as identifying supporting evidence for those facts. The task is divided into two subtasks, each with its own evaluation metrics and datasets. The paper also discusses the evaluation process and provides an overview of the participating teams.

The use of complex numbers in quantum mechanics is a fundamental aspect, yet its underlying justification remains unclear. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive explanation for the necessity of complex numbers in quantum mechanics, drawing on the principles of probability amplitudes and the properties of Hilbert spaces.

This study focuses on the concept of metric dimension in graphs, specifically examining its application to truncated versions of graphs. We establish a relationship between the metric dimension of a graph and its truncated form, and provide a method for calculating the metric dimension of certain types of truncated graphs.

This study derives a set of equations that describe the movement of groundwater over vast distances, taking into account the effects of capillarity and surface tension. The analysis is based on a simplified model of porous media, which is then extended to a more complex system involving a water table and an unsaturated zone. The resulting equations are used to investigate the evolution of the water table and the movement of groundwater over long periods of time.

A novel approach to eliminating sulfur oxides from flue gas is presented, utilizing ozone and ultraviolet light. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through laboratory experiments, which show that ozone can efficiently remove SO2 and SO3 from flue gas, with UV light enhancing the process. The results indicate that the proposed method can achieve high removal rates of sulfur oxides, with minimal energy consumption.

This paper introduces a parallel SystemC virtual platform designed for evaluating neuromorphic architectures, specifically those based on the spiking neural network paradigm. The platform is built upon the SystemC TLM-2.0 standard, enabling efficient simulation of complex neuromorphic systems.

In real-world scenarios, information is often incomplete, making it difficult to make definitive decisions. To address this challenge, we introduce Indecision Trees, a novel decision-making framework that learns to reason under uncertainty. By incorporating a decision-theoretic approach, Indecision Trees can make informed choices even when faced with incomplete information. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Indecision Trees through experiments on various datasets, including the TAC-ASR task, and show that they can achieve state-of-the-art results.

The Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) algorithm is a popular method for measuring the similarity between time series data. However, its high computational cost makes it impractical for large-scale similarity searches. To address this issue, we introduce an early abandoning technique for PrunedDTW, a variant of DTW that uses a pruning strategy to reduce unnecessary computations. Our approach allows PrunedDTW to terminate early when the lower bound of the distance exceeds the current best distance, thereby significantly reducing the number of operations required. Experimental results demonstrate that our early abandoning method can achieve substantial speedups, up to 100 times faster, without compromising the accuracy of the search results.

This study investigates the effectiveness of inquiry-based conceptual feedback in teaching software testing, comparing it to traditional detailed feedback mechanisms. The inquiry-based approach encourages students to identify and correct their own mistakes, while traditional feedback provides specific guidance on how to improve their work. The research involved 120 undergraduate students who were randomly assigned to one of two groups, with each group receiving a different type of feedback. The results showed that students who received inquiry-based conceptual feedback performed better on a post-test, indicating that this method may be more effective in teaching software testing. The study also highlights the importance of providing timely and relevant feedback in software testing education.

Deep neural networks have achieved remarkable success in various tasks, but their complex nature makes them difficult to interpret. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that integrates concept analysis and inductive logic programming to generate more understandable explanations for DNNs. By leveraging the strengths of both methods, our approach can effectively explain the decision-making process of DNNs, even when dealing with complex data types such as images and text.

Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have been widely applied to various graph-related tasks, but their effectiveness diminishes as the number of layers increases due to the over-smoothing issue. This problem arises from the excessive smoothing of node representations, which hinders GCNs from capturing meaningful information. In this study, we delve into the over-smoothing phenomenon and demonstrate that it is a direct consequence of the GCN's graph convolution operation. Furthermore, we propose a novel approach to mitigate over-smoothing by incorporating a learnable parameter into the GCN's convolution operation. This modification enables the network to adaptively control the degree of smoothing, thereby alleviating the over-smoothing problem.

A search for dark matter particles is conducted using data from proton-proton collisions at the LHC, with a total energy of 13 TeV and a dataset size of 137 fb^-1. The analysis focuses on events containing a leptonically decaying Z boson and missing transverse momentum, which could indicate the presence of dark matter. The data is compared to predictions from the Standard Model, and no significant deviation is found. The results are used to set limits on the production of dark matter particles in various models, including simplified models with different mediator masses and spin, as well as models with vector-like dark matter fermions.

We introduce novel transverse momentum dependent (TMD) parton distribution functions, which are based on Wilson lines that extend in the transverse plane. These new distributions are connected to the standard TMDs through a specific relationship. Additionally, we examine the impact of these new distributions on the cross-section for the Drell-Yan process.

We introduce a new class of topological groups, referred to as spaces with socks, which are characterized by a specific property: the product of any two open sets is also open. This property is equivalent to the existence of a continuous homomorphism from the group to a discrete topological group. We demonstrate that spaces with socks are precisely the colimits of finite groups, and we establish a characterization of these groups in terms of their underlying topological structure.

We have successfully grown Heusler films on graphene/sapphire substrates using a remote epitaxy technique. By adjusting the distance between the source and substrate, we can control the balance between remote, pinhole, and van der Waals epitaxy. This allows us to produce high-quality Heusler films with a range of properties.

This research focuses on developing a Bayesian approach for multivariate time series analysis, particularly in scenarios involving heavy-tailed distributions and non-stationary behavior. We introduce a novel model that combines a heavy-tailed distribution with a non-stationary structure, and we demonstrate its effectiveness through both simulated and real-world data examples.

This discovery was made possible by the PEARLS lens model, which accurately predicts the magnification of the star. The star's observed brightness is 100 times greater than expected, indicating a magnification factor of 100. This level of magnification is the highest ever recorded for a star at such a great distance. The star's properties, including its temperature and mass, have been determined to be 3500 Kelvin and 15 times the mass of the Sun, respectively. The star's mass loss rate is estimated to be 10^-4 solar masses per year.
